title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
authors: Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish (equal contribution), Tom Henighan, Tom B. Brown, Benjamin Chess, Rewon Child, Scott Gray, Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, Dario Amodei

code.title: no official release; Porian et al.'s reproduction
code.note: the paper released no code or run data. The closest public material is Porian et al. (2024), who reproduce the Kaplan setup over 900 runs and publish their data and analysis code (README and the notebooks, about 20 minutes)

takeaway: LM loss follows smooth power laws in N, D, and C over 6+ orders of magnitude; prescribed spending compute mostly on model size (N ~ C^0.73) with early stopping, an allocation Chinchilla later corrected to equal N/D scaling (~20 tokens/param).
verdict: Believe the measurements: loss really is a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute, shape barely matters, and bigger models learn from fewer tokens; every later scaling study confirms this. Do not plan with the compute allocation (N growing as C^0.73): it came from one fixed-length training schedule with a long warmup, uncounted output-layer compute and untuned optimisers, and Chinchilla and Porian et al. replaced it with N and D growing equally.
run_label: refit the laws on a toy sweep you can inspect

headline.k: loss falls as N<sup>-0.076</sup> in non-embedding parameters
headline.d: doubling N multiplies the loss by 0.95, over six orders of magnitude

headline.k: the paper's optimal model size for a compute budget
headline.d: 10x compute: 5x bigger model, 2x more data; Chinchilla later found C<sup>0.50</sup>

headline.k: data needed to keep overfitting below seed noise
headline.d: 8x the model needs only about 5x the data

resources.n: modern end-to-end treatment of the scaling-law literature, from Kaplan through Chinchilla to current practice, with the fitting pitfalls spelled out.
accessible walkthrough of the Kaplan and Chinchilla papers side by side, good for building intuition before running a sweep.

resources.t: Resolving Discrepancies in Compute-Optimal Scaling of Language Models
resources.n: the forensic reconciliation of Kaplan and Chinchilla: reproduces Kaplan's 0.88 and 0.73 exponents, then removes them one cause at a time (output-layer FLOPs, warmup length, optimiser tuning) and finds learning-rate decay matters little for the exponent.
what the revised laws imply about data as the binding constraint; a useful counterpoint to this paper's "big models over big data" conclusion.

kb.n: 2022: the direct successor; revises the compute-optimal allocation to equal N and D scaling (about 20 tokens per parameter).
2020: the first frontier model built on these prescriptions (large N, one pass over most data, stopped short of convergence).
2017: the architecture whose parallelism made these compute scales reachable.
2024: fits its own isoFLOP scaling law (405B is about compute-optimal) and deliberately overtrains the smaller models to cheapen inference.
2024: 14.8T tokens for 37B active parameters, the overtrained regime with mixture of experts.
2019: the model parallelism this paper's Discussion calls for to train wide networks.
2025: decay-free schedules with checkpoint merging, one answer to the schedule-length problem behind the Kaplan and Chinchilla disagreement.
